claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by surface segregation of constituent elements having lower melting points and lower surface energies.
Accumulation of these elements at the nanoparticle surface locally reduces cohesive energy.
Reduced surface cohesive energy promotes formation of a liquid-like surface layer before complete melting.
Rapid cooling produces a nominally homogeneous elemental distribution in the nanoparticles.
Controlled annealing or modulation of the quenching rate can induce surface segregation of low-melting-point metals relative to a rapidly quenched baseline.
The relevant nanoparticles are typically 5–50 nm in size.
Heating in an inert or vacuum environment at controlled rates isolates the effect of surface segregation on thermal behavior.
The structural mediator is a chemically inhomogeneous near-surface layer enriched in lower-melting-point components.
The segregated near-surface layer weakens interatomic bonding at the particle surface.
During mild annealing, elements with lower melting points and lower surface energies diffuse preferentially to nanoparticle surfaces.
The segregated surface layer has a lower melting temperature than the particle core and therefore initiates premelting.
With further temperature increase, the premelted layer expands and eventually triggers bulk melting.
Annealed nanoparticles will have lower premelting and complete-melting onset temperatures than rapidly quenched, compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched baseline nanoparticles do not exhibit significant surface segregation.
The hypothesis should hold for 5–50 nm HEA nanoparticles with similar elemental mixtures.
Extreme particle sizes, impurities, or secondary phases may cause deviations by interfering with diffusion.
The magnitude of the temperature shift and the segregation needed for measurable premelting depend on elemental composition and synthesis conditions.
A controlled comparison can use nanoparticles from the same precursor, with one set annealed and the other rapidly quenched.
Premelting onset, complete melting temperature, and surface elemental distribution are the proposed measured variables.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if annealing fails to produce a statistically significant reduction in melting onsets or fails to produce significant surface segregation.
